## Rules and their AWS sources

### Policy Court

| Rule | What it says | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| implicit-deny | A request is denied unless a policy allows it (implicit deny). | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic_policy-eval-denyallow.html |
| explicit-deny | One matching explicit Deny in any applicable policy decides the request: Deny. It overrides every Allow. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic_policy-eval-denyallow.html |
| same-account-union | Inside one account an Allow in the identity-based policy, the resource-based policy, or both is enough. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic.html |
| cross-identity | Across accounts the principal needs an identity-based Allow in its own account. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic-cross-account.html |
| cross-resource | Across accounts the resource-based policy in the resource account must also allow the principal. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic-cross-account.html |
| cross-both | A cross-account request is allowed only when both accounts allow it. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic-cross-account.html |
| boundary-limits | A permissions boundary only limits what identity-based policies can grant. It never grants. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_boundaries.html |
| boundary-intersect | Identity-based permissions and the boundary combine as an intersection: both must allow. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_boundaries.html |
| boundary-user-resource | Same account: a resource-based Allow that names the IAM user ARN is not limited by an implicit deny in the boundary or identity-based policy. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_boundaries.html |
| boundary-role-resource | Same account: a resource-based Allow that names the IAM role ARN is limited by an implicit deny in the boundary or session policy. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_boundaries.html |
| session-direct | Same account: a resource-based Allow that names the role session ARN is granted directly to the session and is not limited by the boundary, identity-based or session policy. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_boundaries.html |
| session-limits | A session policy only limits the session. It never grants. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies.html |
| scp-no-grant | A service control policy never grants permissions; it only sets the maximum. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps.html |
| scp-every-level | Every organization level (root, each OU on the path, the account) needs an Allow in its SCP, or the request is denied. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps_evaluation.html |
| scp-deny-any-level | A Deny in an SCP at any level of the path denies the request. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps_evaluation.html |
| scp-scope | An SCP applies to the principals of the account it governs, not to principals of other accounts. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic_policy-eval-denyallow.html |
| scp-management | SCPs do not affect principals in the organization management account. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps.html |
| scp-allow-resource | An Allow in an SCP can only name "*" as its Resource. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps_syntax.html |
| trust-exception | Same account: a role trust policy or key policy must itself allow the principal; an identity-based Allow alone is not enough. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic_policy-eval-denyallow.html |
| principal-session | The requester in a role session is the session ARN; a policy naming the role ARN matches that role session. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies_boundaries.html |
| principal-account | An account ID or the account root ARN as Principal delegates to every principal of that account. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_principal.html |
| principal-all | Principal "*" matches every principal. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_principal.html |
| principal-partial | A Principal cannot use a wildcard for part of a name or ARN, so such a policy is refused. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_principal.html |
| principal-identity | Identity-based policies have no Principal element (a policy written otherwise is refused). | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_principal.html |
| scp-no-principal | SCPs have no Principal element (a policy written otherwise is refused). | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_scps_syntax.html |
| action-wildcard | Actions may use * as a wildcard inside the action name. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_action.html |
| action-case | Action prefix and name are not case sensitive. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_action.html |
| resource-wildcard | In a Resource ARN, * stands for any run of characters, including /. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_resource.html |
| resource-wildcard-colon | A * that is the last character of an ARN segment can also match beyond the colon. A * in the middle of a segment is not settled, so such a Resource is refused. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_resource.html |
| cond-missing-key | A condition whose key is missing from the request is false (except ...IfExists). | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_condition_operators.html |
| cond-ifexists | With an ...IfExists operator a missing key makes the condition true. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_condition_operators.html |
| cond-ip | aws:SourceIp is the address the request comes from. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_condition_operators.html |
| cond-cidr | IP ranges in a condition are written in CIDR format (IPv4 only here). | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_condition_operators.html |
| cond-ip-operators | IpAddress matches an address inside the range; NotIpAddress matches every address outside it. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_condition_operators.html |
| cond-mfa | aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is absent for requests made with long-term access keys. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_condition-keys.html |
| cond-bool | Bool compares a key with true or false. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_condition_operators.html |
| cond-tls | aws:SecureTransport is false when the request was not sent over TLS. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_condition-keys.html |
| cond-orgid | aws:PrincipalOrgID is present only for principals in an organization member account; StringEquals compares it exactly. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_condition-keys.html |
| cond-string | StringEquals is an exact, case-sensitive match. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_condition_operators.html |

### Packet Tracer

| Rule | What it says | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| route-local | Every route table has a local route for the VPC CIDR, so traffic inside the VPC is delivered locally. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/subnet-route-tables.html |
| route-main | A subnet with no explicit route table association uses the main route table. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/subnet-route-tables.html |
| route-longest | The most specific (longest prefix) route that matches the destination wins. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/route-tables-priority.html |
| igw-attach | An internet gateway must be attached to the VPC and routed to; without one nothing reaches the internet. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/VPC_Internet_Gateway.html |
| igw-public-subnet | A subnet is public only if its route table has a route to the internet gateway. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/VPC_Internet_Gateway.html |
| igw-no-route | Without a route to the internet gateway, an instance cannot talk to the internet, even with a public IP address. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/VPC_Internet_Gateway.html |
| igw-public-ip | An instance needs a public IPv4 address (or Elastic IP) to use the internet gateway. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/VPC_Internet_Gateway.html |
| igw-inbound | Internet clients can start a connection to an instance in a public subnet through its public IPv4 address. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/VPC_Internet_Gateway.html |
| nat-private-route | A private subnet reaches the internet through a NAT gateway only if its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to it. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/route-table-options.html |
| nat-public-subnet | A public NAT gateway is created in a public subnet. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-nat-gateway.html |
| nat-to-igw | The NAT gateway forwards traffic to the internet through the internet gateway of its VPC. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-nat-gateway.html |
| nat-outbound-only | A NAT gateway is outbound only: connections must start inside the VPC, so the internet cannot start one to a private instance. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-nat-gateway.html |
| nat-nacl | A network ACL controls the traffic to and from the NAT gateway subnet. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/nat-gateway-basics.html |
| nat-ports | Replies to a NAT gateway arrive on ports 1024-65535. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/custom-network-acl.html |
| nat-no-peering | Traffic cannot be routed to a NAT gateway through a VPC peering connection. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/nat-gateway-basics.html |
| gwep-no-igw | A gateway endpoint gives access to Amazon S3 or DynamoDB without an internet gateway or NAT device. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/gateway-endpoints.html |
| gwep-route | A subnet uses a gateway endpoint only if its route table has the service prefix list route to the endpoint. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/gateway-endpoints.html |
| gwep-unassociated | Subnets whose route tables are not associated with the endpoint use the public service endpoint instead. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/gateway-endpoints.html |
| gwep-precedence | The endpoint route beats a 0.0.0.0/0 internet gateway route for that service; other traffic keeps using the internet gateway route. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/gateway-endpoints.html |
| gwep-other-service | A gateway endpoint route covers only its own service; traffic for a different service follows the other routes. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/gateway-endpoints.html |
| gwep-sg | Security groups of instances using a gateway endpoint must still allow traffic to and from the service. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/gateway-endpoints.html |
| gwep-prefix-sg | A security group rule can name the service prefix list. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpc-endpoints-s3.html |
| gwep-prefix-sg-ddb | A security group rule can name the DynamoDB prefix list. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpc-endpoints-ddb.html |
| gwep-nacl-ddb | The network ACL of the subnet must still allow traffic to and from DynamoDB. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpc-endpoints-ddb.html |
| gwep-nacl | The network ACL of the subnet must still allow traffic to and from the service. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpc-endpoints-s3.html |
| ifep-eni | An interface endpoint is a network interface with a private IP address in each chosen subnet. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/create-interface-endpoint.html |
| ifep-sg | The interface endpoint's own security group must allow the clients' traffic. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/create-interface-endpoint.html |
| ifep-nacl | Network ACLs must allow traffic between the clients and the endpoint network interfaces. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/create-interface-endpoint.html |
| sg-allow-only | Security groups only allow; a rule can never deny, so traffic with no matching allow rule is dropped. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/security-group-rules.html |
| sg-inbound-none | A security group with no inbound rules allows no inbound traffic. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/security-group-rules.html |
| sg-outbound-default | A new security group allows all outbound traffic until that rule is removed. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/security-group-rules.html |
| sg-outbound-none | Outbound traffic needs a matching outbound rule once the default rule is replaced. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/security-group-rules.html |
| sg-aggregate | With several security groups on one resource, their rules are combined: any one allow is enough. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/security-group-rules.html |
| sg-stateful | Security groups are stateful: replies to allowed traffic are allowed whatever the rules in the other direction say. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-security-groups.html |
| sg-stateful-reply | Security groups are stateful: the reply to a request an instance sends is allowed back in whatever the inbound rules say. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-security-groups.html |
| sg-reference | A rule that names a security group applies to every instance associated with that group. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/security-group-rules.html |
| sg-reference-peer | In one Region, a rule can name a security group of the peer VPC. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/peering/vpc-peering-basics.html |
| nacl-assoc | A subnet with no explicit network ACL association uses the default network ACL. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-network-acls.html |
| nacl-order | Network ACL rules are checked from the lowest rule number upward. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-network-acls.html |
| nacl-first-match | The first matching rule decides; later rules are not looked at. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-network-acls.html |
| nacl-allow-deny | A network ACL rule can allow or deny. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-network-acls.html |
| nacl-stateless | Network ACLs are stateless: the return traffic needs its own allow rule in the other direction. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-network-acls.html |
| nacl-boundary | Network ACLs are checked when traffic enters or leaves a subnet, not for traffic inside one subnet. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-network-acls.html |
| nacl-default | The default network ACL allows all traffic in and out. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/default-network-acl.html |
| nacl-final-deny | A packet that matches no numbered rule is denied by the final * rule (so a custom network ACL with no allow rules denies everything). | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/custom-network-acl.html |
| nacl-response | Every allowed flow needs a rule that allows the response traffic. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/custom-network-acl.html |
| eph-client | The client that opens the connection picks the ephemeral port range for the replies. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/custom-network-acl.html |
| eph-linux | Many Linux kernels, including the Amazon Linux kernel, use ports 32768-61000 for replies; the scenarios use Amazon Linux clients. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/custom-network-acl.html |
| eph-windows | A Windows Server 2008 or later client uses ports 49152-65535. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/custom-network-acl.html |
| peer-routes | Peering carries traffic only if the route tables on both sides point the peer CIDR at the peering connection. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/peering/vpc-peering-basics.html |
| peer-overlap | VPCs with overlapping CIDR blocks cannot be peered, so such a layout is refused. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/peering/vpc-peering-basics.html |
| peer-non-transitive | Peering is not transitive: a VPC cannot reach a second peer through the VPC between them. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/peering/vpc-peering-basics.html |
| peer-no-other | There is no peering relationship with a VPC that is not directly peered. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/peering/vpc-peering-basics.html |
| peer-edge-igw | A peer cannot use this VPC's internet gateway to reach the internet. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/peering/vpc-peering-basics.html |
| peer-edge-nat | A peer cannot use this VPC's NAT device to reach the internet. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/peering/vpc-peering-basics.html |
| peer-edge-gwep | A peer cannot use this VPC's gateway endpoint to reach Amazon S3. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/peering/vpc-peering-basics.html |

### Disaster Bunker drill

| Rule | What it says | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cost-order | The four strategies are listed in increasing order of cost and complexity, and decreasing order of RTO and RPO: backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, multi-site active/active. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reliability-pillar/rel_planning_for_recovery_disaster_recovery.html |
| class-backup-restore | Backup and restore: RPO in hours, RTO in 24 hours or less. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reliability-pillar/rel_planning_for_recovery_disaster_recovery.html |
| class-pilot-light | Pilot light: RPO in minutes, RTO in tens of minutes. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reliability-pillar/rel_planning_for_recovery_disaster_recovery.html |
| class-warm-standby | Warm standby: RPO in seconds, RTO in minutes. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reliability-pillar/rel_planning_for_recovery_disaster_recovery.html |
| class-active-active | Multi-site active/active: RPO near zero, RTO potentially zero. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reliability-pillar/rel_planning_for_recovery_disaster_recovery.html |
| tradeoff | Choosing a strategy trades lower downtime and data loss against cost and complexity, so the pick is the least costly strategy whose RPO and RTO classes both meet the targets. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reliability-pillar/rel_planning_for_recovery_disaster_recovery.html |
| pitr-backups | Automated or continuous backups with point-in-time recovery can lower the backup-and-restore RPO to as low as 5 minutes in some cases, so an RPO in minutes with such backups is not settled by the class table (refused). | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reliability-pillar/rel_planning_for_recovery_disaster_recovery.html |
| blocks-cumulative-warm | Warm standby also uses the services of backup and restore and pilot light, so the blocks of cheaper strategies are already in place and are not what a strategy adds. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-options-in-the-cloud.html |
| blocks-cumulative-active | Active/active also uses the services of the three cheaper strategies, so each strategy is asked for what it adds. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-options-in-the-cloud.html |
| block-pit-backups | Backup and restore adds: Point-in-time backups of data (for example Amazon EBS or Amazon RDS snapshots). | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-options-in-the-cloud.html |
| block-backup-copy | Backup and restore adds: AWS Backup copies of the backups sent to the recovery Region. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-options-in-the-cloud.html |
| block-iac-redeploy | Backup and restore adds: AWS CloudFormation templates that redeploy the infrastructure at recovery time. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-options-in-the-cloud.html |
| block-ami-copy | Backup and restore adds: Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) copied to the recovery Region. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-options-in-the-cloud.html |
| block-cont-replication | Pilot light adds: Continuous cross-Region data replication (for example Aurora global database or DynamoDB global tables). | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-options-in-the-cloud.html |
| block-data-tier-on | Pilot light adds: Databases and object storage always on in the recovery Region. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-options-in-the-cloud.html |
| block-app-servers-off | Pilot light adds: Application servers prepared but switched off until failover. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-options-in-the-cloud.html |
| block-scaled-down-stack | Warm standby adds: A scaled-down but fully functional copy of production, always running in the recovery Region. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-options-in-the-cloud.html |
| block-scale-up-failover | Warm standby adds: A failover that only needs scaling up, because everything is already deployed and running. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reliability-pillar/rel_planning_for_recovery_disaster_recovery.html |
| block-reduced-capacity-traffic | Warm standby adds: A recovery Region that can serve traffic at reduced capacity immediately. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-options-in-the-cloud.html |
| block-all-regions-serve | Multi-site active/active adds: The workload running and serving traffic in every Region it is deployed to. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-options-in-the-cloud.html |
| block-user-routing-policies | Multi-site active/active adds: Routing policies (Route 53 or Global Accelerator) that decide which users reach which active Region. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-options-in-the-cloud.html |
| block-multi-region-writes | Multi-site active/active adds: A design for data consistency when writes can land in each active Region. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-options-in-the-cloud.html |

### Cold Cellar planner

| Rule | What it says | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cls-standard | Data read more than once a month, with millisecond access, belongs in S3 Standard. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html |
| cls-standard-ia | Long-lived data read about once a month with millisecond access fits S3 Standard-IA. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html |
| cls-onezone-recreatable | S3 One Zone-IA is for infrequently read data you can re-create if the Availability Zone fails. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html |
| cls-onezone-cheaper | S3 One Zone-IA keeps data in one Availability Zone and is less expensive than S3 Standard-IA. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html |
| cls-onezone-loss | S3 One Zone-IA is not resilient to the loss of the Availability Zone, so data that cannot be re-created goes in S3 Standard-IA. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html |
| cls-intelligent-tiering | S3 Intelligent-Tiering is the class for data with unknown or changing access patterns. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html |
| cls-glacier-ir | S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval serves archive data that is read about once a quarter, or rarely, and must open in milliseconds. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/glacier-storage-classes.html |
| cls-glacier-ir-rare | Rarely read archive data that still needs millisecond retrieval goes in S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html |
| cls-glacier-fr | S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval is for archives where parts of the data may be needed in minutes; objects must be restored before they can be read. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html |
| cls-glacier-da | S3 Glacier Deep Archive is for archive data read less than once a year when retrieval times of hours are acceptable. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html |
| restore-first | Objects in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and S3 Glacier Deep Archive must be restored before they can be read, so they never serve milliseconds reads. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html |
| min-duration-ia | S3 Standard-IA and S3 One Zone-IA have a 30-day minimum storage duration; deleting or moving an object earlier still charges for 30 days. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html |
| min-duration-glacier | S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval and Flexible Retrieval have a 90-day minimum storage duration; S3 Glacier Deep Archive has 180 days. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/glacier-storage-classes.html |
| single-rule-min-duration | One Lifecycle rule cannot move an object out of a class before its minimum storage duration has passed, so the next move waits until then. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html |
| single-rule-example | Documented example: after 4 days in S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval (90-day minimum), the move to S3 Glacier Deep Archive must come at day 94 or later. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html |
| waterfall | Lifecycle transitions follow a waterfall: an object only moves toward colder classes, never back up. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html |
| wf-standard | From S3 Standard a rule can move objects to any other class on this list. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html |
| wf-standard-ia | From S3 Standard-IA a rule can move objects to S3 Intelligent-Tiering, One Zone-IA or any Glacier class, but not back to S3 Standard. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html |
| wf-intelligent-tiering | From S3 Intelligent-Tiering a rule can move objects to S3 One Zone-IA or a Glacier class. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html |
| wf-onezone-ia | From S3 One Zone-IA a rule can move objects only to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html |
| wf-glacier-ir | From S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval a rule can move objects only to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html |
| wf-glacier-fr | From S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval a rule can move objects only to S3 Glacier Deep Archive. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html |
| wf-glacier-da | A Lifecycle rule cannot move objects out of S3 Glacier Deep Archive to any other class. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/lifecycle-transition-general-considerations.html |
| min-billable-size | For an object smaller than the minimum billable size, S3 Standard-IA and S3 One Zone-IA charge for that minimum size. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html |
| ia-larger-objects | S3 Standard-IA and S3 One Zone-IA suit objects larger than the minimum billable size that are kept at least 30 days. | https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html |

## One sample per type

### Policy Court: puzzle-policy-court-003 (Shirley creates a user, level 2, identity-keep)

Shirley should manage only Amazon S3, Amazon CloudWatch and Amazon EC2, so she has a permissions boundary. Later an administrator attached a policy that allows her to create IAM users.

**The request**

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Principal | arn:aws:iam::ACCT_MAIN:user/Shirley |
| Action | iam:CreateUser |
| Resource | arn:aws:iam::ACCT_MAIN:user/new-hire |
| Accounts | Same account (ACCT_MAIN) |
| aws:SourceIp | not in the request |
| aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent | not in the request (long-term access keys) |
| aws:SecureTransport | true |
| aws:PrincipalOrgID | not in the request (account is not in an organization) |

**Reading the exhibit**

```
Account names such as ACCT_DEV stand for 12-digit account IDs. Every policy that exists for this request is listed; some may not apply.
```

**Identity-based policy: Policy on the user Shirley**

```
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "iam:CreateUser",
      "Resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}
```

**Permissions boundary: Shirley's permissions boundary**

```
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "s3:*",
        "cloudwatch:*",
        "ec2:*"
      ],
      "Resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}
```

- What is the result of this request?
  - Computed answer: Deny
- Which policy decided it? An explicit Deny: the policy that holds it. Otherwise: the single policy that, if its Allow applied (its condition met, the missing action added, the principal named), would by itself turn the result into Allow. A boundary, a service control policy level or a session policy counts when it is the one lacking the Allow, but none of them ever grants. Pick "No single policy" when no one policy could do it alone (for example two sides would both have to change, or several policies are equally able) or none exists.
  - Computed answer: Permissions boundary: Shirley's permissions boundary

**Why:**
- The boundary "Shirley's permissions boundary" has no Allow for this action.
- No Allow applies to this request, so it is an implicit deny.

### Packet Tracer: puzzle-packet-tracer-003 (The wrong tier in the rule, level 2, gatehouse)

The database security group admits the web tier by name. An application server in a different tier tries to open a database connection over the local network.

**Shop VPC**

```
CIDR 10.0.0.0/16. No internet gateway is attached.
```

**Shop VPC: subnets**

| Subnet | CIDR | Route table | Network ACL |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| web-sub | 10.0.1.0/24 | none associated | none associated |
| app-sub | 10.0.2.0/24 | none associated | none associated |
| db-sub | 10.0.3.0/24 | none associated | none associated |

**Shop VPC: route tables**

| Route table | Destination | Target |
| --- | --- | --- |
| main-rt (main) | 10.0.0.0/16 | local |

**Shop VPC: security groups (allow rules only)**

| Security group | Direction | Protocol | Ports | Source or destination |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| web-sg | inbound | TCP | 443 | 0.0.0.0/0 |
| web-sg | outbound | all | all | 0.0.0.0/0 |
| app-sg | inbound | TCP | 8080 | group web-sg |
| app-sg | outbound | all | all | 0.0.0.0/0 |
| db-sg | inbound | TCP | 5432 | group web-sg |
| db-sg | outbound | all | all | 0.0.0.0/0 |

**Shop VPC: network ACLs**

| Network ACL | Direction | Rule | Protocol | Ports | Source or destination | Action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| nacl-default (default) | inbound | 100 | all | all | 0.0.0.0/0 | ALLOW |
| nacl-default (default) | inbound | * | all | all | 0.0.0.0/0 | DENY |
| nacl-default (default) | outbound | 100 | all | all | 0.0.0.0/0 | ALLOW |
| nacl-default (default) | outbound | * | all | all | 0.0.0.0/0 | DENY |

**Shop VPC: instances and endpoints**

| Name | Type | Subnet | Private IP | Public IPv4 | Security groups |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| web-1 | instance | web-sub | 10.0.1.10 | none | web-sg |
| app-1 | instance | app-sub | 10.0.2.10 | none | app-sg |
| db-1 | instance | db-sub | 10.0.3.10 | none | db-sg |

**The connection attempt**

```
From: app-1 at 10.0.2.10. To: db-1 at 10.0.3.10. TCP on port 5432. The source opens the connection. The client runs Amazon Linux. Assume the service or application at the destination accepts the connection, that IAM and bucket policies are not involved, and that any endpoint policy is the default (full access).
```

- Does this connection attempt succeed?
  - Computed answer: No, the connection fails
- Which one component blocks it? Name the first component on the packet's path that cannot carry it (for a route table, the one the subnet actually uses; for peering that cannot carry the traffic, the peering connection). Choose "Nothing blocks it" if the connection succeeds.
  - Computed answer: Security group db-sg

**Why:**
- app-sub has no explicit route table, so it uses the main route table main-rt.
- app-sub has no explicit network ACL, so it uses the default nacl-default.
- app-sg allows TCP 5432 to db-1 out of app-1.
- app-sub outbound: TCP 5432 to db-1: nacl-default allows everything.
- main-rt sends db-1 to local (10.0.0.0/16).
- db-sub inbound: TCP 5432 from app-1: nacl-default allows everything.
- db-sg has no rule that allows TCP 5432 from app-1 into db-1.
- The reply to allowed inbound traffic leaves db-1 whatever its outbound rules say.
- The client chooses the reply (ephemeral) ports: Linux uses 32768-61000.
- A Linux client's replies come back on ports 32768-61000.
- Network ACLs are stateless, so each reply is checked against its own rules.
- db-sub outbound: reply to app-1 on ports 32768-61000: nacl-default allows everything.
- main-rt delivers the reply locally.
- app-sub inbound: reply from db-1 on ports 32768-61000: nacl-default allows everything.
- The reply to app-1's request is allowed in whatever its inbound rules say.

### Disaster Bunker drill: puzzle-disaster-bunker-003 (Ferry tickets, level 1, disaster-bunker)

A ticketing service needs data loss measured in seconds and recovery in minutes. Pick the least costly strategy.

**Workload**

```
Ticketing service with web, application and database tiers.
```

**Targets**

| Measure | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Recovery point objective (RPO) | In seconds |
| Recovery time objective (RTO) | minutes |
| Cost constraint | The least costly strategy that meets both targets. |

**Documented classes (increasing cost)**

| Strategy | RPO | RTO |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Backup and restore | hours | 24 hours or less |
| Pilot light | minutes | tens of minutes |
| Warm standby | seconds | minutes |
| Multi-site active/active | near zero | potentially zero |

- Which is the least costly DR strategy that meets both targets and the cost constraint?
  - Computed answer: Warm standby
- Which building blocks does your chosen strategy add to those of the cheaper strategies? Select all that apply.
  - Computed answer: A scaled-down but fully functional copy of production, always running in the recovery Region | A failover that only needs scaling up, because everything is already deployed and running | A recovery Region that can serve traffic at reduced capacity immediately

**Why:**
- Cost and complexity rise in the order backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, multi-site active/active.
- An RPO in seconds is first met by Warm standby.
- An RTO of minutes is first met by Warm standby.
- The stricter target decides, and the least costly strategy meeting both is Warm standby.
- Warm standby also uses the blocks of the two cheaper strategies; only what it adds is selected.
- Warm standby adds: A scaled-down but fully functional copy of production, always running in the recovery Region.
- Warm standby adds: A failover that only needs scaling up, because everything is already deployed and running.
- Warm standby adds: A recovery Region that can serve traffic at reduced capacity immediately.

### Cold Cellar planner: puzzle-cold-cellar-003 (Thumbnails that can be redrawn, level 1, cold-cellar)

A photo site stores generated thumbnails. For the first month they load constantly. Afterwards each thumbnail is fetched about once a month and must still open instantly. If a thumbnail is lost, a job regenerates it from the original photo. Pick the classes and the day of the move.

**Objects**

```
Generated JPEG thumbnails. Average object size: 512 KB. Days are counted from the day each object is created.
```

**Access over time**

| Stage | Starts on day | Access | Retrieval need | Can be re-created? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0 | Read many times a month | Must open immediately (milliseconds) | Yes |
| 2 | 30 | Read about once a month | Must open immediately (milliseconds) | Yes |

- Storage class for stage 1 (set when the objects are uploaded): the least expensive class whose documented use case fits
  - Computed answer: S3 Standard
- Storage class for stage 2: the least expensive class whose documented use case fits
  - Computed answer: S3 One Zone-IA
- Day (counted from object creation) of the one Lifecycle rule that moves objects to stage 2: the earliest day that is both at or after the stage start and free of any early-move charge
  - Computed answer: Day 30

**Why:**
- Stage 1: Read more than once a month with millisecond access: S3 Standard.
- Stage 2: Read about monthly and can be re-created: S3 One Zone-IA, the less expensive of the two infrequent-access classes.
- Stage 2: Read about monthly and can be re-created: S3 One Zone-IA, the less expensive of the two infrequent-access classes.
- Stage 1 to 2: S3 Standard to S3 One Zone-IA is a supported move.

### Purchase Planner: puzzle-purchase-planner-003 (Steady, but no promises, level 2, counting-house)

A production API runs around the clock and has done so for years. Company policy forbids any purchase commitment, and the API cannot be interrupted. The tempting answer is a plan, but the policy decides.

**Workload profile**

| Property | Value |
| --- | --- |
| How long it runs | Steady use around the clock for at least a year |
| Can it be interrupted? | No |
| Willing to commit to | No commitment of any kind |
| Expected to change | Nothing |
| Capacity need | None |
| Manual exchanges or modifications | Acceptable |
| Goal when several plans fit | No stated preference |

- Which purchasing model does this profile call for?
  - Computed answer: On-Demand Instances

**Why:**
- No commitment is wanted and On-Demand needs none.

### Architecture Builder: puzzle-architecture-builder-003 (Decouple order intake, level 2, blueprint-hall)

An order site must keep taking orders even when the order-processing instances are slow. The processing tier is stateless and runs in private subnets across zones.

**Requirements**

```
1. The web/app instances must not have public addresses: they sit in private app subnets behind the load balancer.
2. The stateless web tier must survive the loss of one Availability Zone: run instances in at least two zones.
3. Order submission must keep working when the processing tier is slow or down: decouple the tiers with a managed queue: put a queue in the regional row, with at least one app instance in a private app subnet as the worker behind it.
```

**How scoring works**

```
You do not have to use every component. The design is scored only against the requirements above, each by an explicit check; full credit needs every check to pass.
```

**Components you can place**

| Component | How many |
| --- | --- |
| Application Load Balancer node | 2 |
| Web/app instance (Auto Scaling group) | 3 |
| NAT gateway | 2 |
| Amazon RDS primary DB instance | 1 |
| Amazon RDS standby DB instance | 1 |
| Amazon ElastiCache node | 2 |
| Amazon SQS queue | 1 |

**Zones**

```
2 Availability Zones (Zone A, Zone B).
```


**Why:**
- The web/app instances must not have public addresses: they sit in private app subnets behind the load balancer. Instances: 2; in private app subnets: 2.
- The stateless web tier must survive the loss of one Availability Zone: run instances in at least two zones. Zones with instances: 2.
- Order submission must keep working when the processing tier is slow or down: decouple the tiers with a managed queue: put a queue in the regional row, with at least one app instance in a private app subnet as the worker behind it. Queues in the regional row: 1; app instances in private app subnets (the workers behind the queue): 2.

### Qualifier Sprint: puzzle-qualifier-sprint-003 (The orders database, level 2, town-charter)

A small online shop needs a MySQL-compatible relational database for its orders. The load is flat around the clock and will stay that way for years, and the team prefers not to size or resize instances by hand. Every design below stores the orders correctly; read the qualifier to see which one fits.

**The designs**

| Design | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| A | MySQL installed on an EC2 instance that your team patches and backs up |
| B | RDS for MySQL, single instance, in private subnets with storage encrypted using a KMS key |
| C | An Aurora Serverless v2 DB cluster |
| D | RDS for MySQL, Multi-AZ DB instance deployment |
| E | RDS for MySQL, single instance, with a reserved DB instance covering its constant use |

- LEAST operational overhead: which design fits best?
  - Computed answer: An Aurora Serverless v2 DB cluster
- MOST cost-effective: which design fits best?
  - Computed answer: RDS for MySQL, single instance, with a reserved DB instance covering its constant use
- MOST secure: which design fits best?
  - Computed answer: RDS for MySQL, single instance, in private subnets with storage encrypted using a KMS key
- HIGHEST availability: which design fits best?
  - Computed answer: RDS for MySQL, Multi-AZ DB instance deployment

**Why:**
- LEAST operational overhead: An Aurora Serverless v2 DB cluster
- MOST cost-effective: RDS for MySQL, single instance, with a reserved DB instance covering its constant use
- MOST secure: RDS for MySQL, single instance, in private subnets with storage encrypted using a KMS key
- HIGHEST availability: RDS for MySQL, Multi-AZ DB instance deployment
